theme: Joy in prison; the Christ hymn; Timothy and Epaphroditus
readingInstruction: Read Philippians 1:1-2:30. Paul writes from prison, yet the letter is full of joy. Notice how he handles his imprisonment, the prayer he offers, the call to unity and humility, and the great Christ hymn in 2:5-11.
settingTheScene: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia where Paul planted the first church in Europe (Acts 16). The church had supported him generously. Now in prison, perhaps in Rome, he writes to thank them, to report on his situation, and to encourage them. Philippians has a repeated theme of joy; the words “joy” and “rejoice” appear about sixteen times. Its message is that joy does not depend on circumstances but on Christ.
observation: “And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (1:6).
“I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel” (1:12).
“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21).
“Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ” (1:27).
“Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves” (2:3).
“Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus” (2:5).
“And every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (2:11).
“For it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (2:13).
interpretation:
Paul’s greeting includes “overseers and deacons.” He thanks God every time he remembers them, because of their partnership in the gospel from the first day. Then the great assurance of verse 6: “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.” The Christian’s confidence rests on God’s faithfulness. He prays that their love may abound with knowledge and discernment, so that they may approve what is excellent and be filled with the fruit of righteousness.

Paul reports on his imprisonment. It has “really served to advance the gospel.” The whole imperial guard knows that his chains are for Christ, and most of the brothers have become more bold to speak the word without fear. Some preach Christ from envy and rivalry, others from good will. Paul’s response is remarkable: “What does it matter? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in that I rejoice.” The gospel is bigger than his reputation. Then he faces death honestly: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” He is torn between wanting to depart and be with Christ, which is far better, and remaining for their sake. He is convinced he will remain.

He calls them to unity and courage: “Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ… standing firm in one spirit, with one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel, and not frightened in anything by your opponents.” Suffering is a gift: “It has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake.”

Then Paul calls for humility, with Christ as the model. “Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others. Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus.” The hymn follows, which we will study in the next doctrinal pause: Christ, in the form of God, emptied himself, took the form of a servant, humbled himself to death on a cross; therefore God exalted him, and every knee will bow.

The practical conclusion: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. Do all things without grumbling or disputing, that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish… among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast to the word of life.” Paul also commends Timothy, who genuinely cares for their welfare, and Epaphroditus, who nearly died for the work of Christ. These are models of Christ’s mind in action.
connection: Acts 16:11-40 tells of the founding of the Philippian church. Isaiah 45:22-23 is the source of 2:10-11. Romans 8:28 and 2 Corinthians 4:7-12 speak of God working in suffering. Philippians 4:10-20 speaks of their gift. John 13:1-17 shows Jesus’ servant act. 1 Peter 2:21-25 calls us to follow his example. 2 Corinthians 8:9 speaks of his becoming poor. Matthew 5:14-16 calls us the light of the world. Hebrews 12:1-3 points to Jesus as pioneer and perfecter.
application:
Read the letter with an eye for the word “joy.” Count how many times it appears.

Look for a way to count someone else more significant this week.

Entrust to God a work that you worry about. He who began it will complete it.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for beginning a good work in you and bringing it to completion.
Tell him what it means that to live is Christ and to die is gain.
Ask him to give you Christ’s humility.
